title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW THE PATRIARCHS TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES—IF THAT WAS NEVER HIS DESIGN?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD ALLOW THE PATRIARCHS TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES—IF THAT WAS NEVER HIS DESIGN?

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob married Leah and Rachel and fathered children through their servants. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why didn’t God stop them? The answer is more uncomfortable—and more beautiful—than simply saying, “That was the Old Testament.”
There is a question many Christians have quietly carried but were afraid to ask out loud.
Maybe you have carried it too.
You read Genesis.
You meet Abraham—the man Scripture calls the father of all who believe.
Then Hagar enters the story.
You meet Jacob—the man whose name becomes Israel.
Then there is Leah.
Rachel.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
You keep reading.
David appears.
A man after God's own heart...yet surrounded by multiple wives.
Then Solomon arrives with a household so enormous that modern readers almost cannot comprehend it.
And somewhere between Sunday school and serious Bible reading, an uncomfortable question begins scratching at the door of your faith:
“If God designed marriage to be between one man and one woman...why did He allow His own patriarchs and kings to practice polygamy?”
And beneath that question is another one.
A more dangerous one.
“Did God change His mind?”
No.
But to understand why, we have to stop confusing something the Bible records with something God recommends.
That distinction changes everything.
Because the Bible is brutally honest about its heroes.
It does not airbrush Abraham.
It does not sanitize Jacob.
It does not protect David's reputation.
It does not edit Solomon's failures out of the story.
Scripture does something far more astonishing.
It shows us sinful human beings as they really were...
and then shows us a holy God continuing His redemptive work in spite of them.
That is not divine approval of everything they did.
That is grace.
And perhaps that is why this question matters far more than polygamy.
Because sooner or later, you are going to discover that the Bible is filled with people God used despite things in their lives God never intended as His ideal.
And then...
if you are courageous enough...
you will realize you are one of them.
Before Abraham ever took Hagar...
before Jacob ever found himself caught between two sisters...
before David built a complicated household...
before Solomon accumulated wives until his heart wandered...
God had already shown humanity what marriage was meant to be.
You have to go back before the patriarchs.
Before Israel.
Before Moses.
Before kings.
Before human civilization learned how to normalize its brokenness.
Go back to Eden.
Genesis 2:24 says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immōw, wəḏāḇaq bə’ištōw, wəhāyū ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
“For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Listen carefully to the language.
בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — bə’ištōw
“His wife.”
And then:
לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ
“One flesh.”
One covenant union.
Before sin distorted human relationships, God presented Adam and Eve.
Not Adam, Eve, and several additional wives.
The pattern appears before the fall.
And that matters.
Then Genesis does something fascinating.
The first explicit polygamist mentioned in Scripture is not Abraham.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 tells us that Lamech “took two wives.”
Read the surrounding story carefully and the atmosphere is not one of spiritual advancement.
Humanity is descending deeper into violence, pride, vengeance, domination, and rebellion.
Lamech eventually boasts about killing a man.
Polygamy enters the biblical narrative not as a new command from heaven but within a world increasingly fractured by sin.
Then Abraham comes.
God promises Abraham descendants.
But years pass.
Sarah remains barren.
The promise seems impossible.
And human beings do what human beings have been doing ever since Eden:
they attempt to accomplish God's purposes through human control.
Sarah gives Hagar to Abraham.
Hagar conceives.
And almost immediately...
the house begins to bleed.
Genesis does not need to insert a sentence saying, “Polygamy causes problems.”
The story shows you.
Jealousy.
Contempt.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
A vulnerable woman running into the wilderness.
A child eventually separated from his father.
Sarah hurts.
Hagar hurts.
Abraham hurts.
Ishmael hurts.
And generations feel the consequences of people trying to manufacture what God had promised to provide.
That is one of Scripture's most sobering methods of teaching.
Sometimes God gives a command.
Sometimes He lets the consequences preach.
Then comes Jacob.
And if anyone tries to use Jacob's household as an advertisement for polygamy, they have not read the story slowly enough.
Jacob loves Rachel.
He is deceived into marrying Leah.
Then Rachel becomes his wife as well.
Then Bilhah enters.
Then Zilpah.
And suddenly the home becomes a battlefield of comparison.
One woman desperate to be loved.
Another desperate to have children.
Servants brought into reproductive rivalry.
Children becoming symbols in their mothers' struggle for affection and status.
Even the naming of children sometimes carries the emotional scars of women trying to be seen.
This is not paradise.
This is heartbreak with a family tree.
God works through that family.
But do not confuse God's ability to redeem dysfunction with God's endorsement of dysfunction.
That distinction is absolutely essential.
God can bring holiness out of wreckage without calling the wreckage holy.
God can fulfill His promises through broken people without declaring their broken choices righteous.
God can write redemption through a dysfunctional family without pretending the dysfunction was His original design.
That is grace.
And then the Law comes.
Here the question becomes even more difficult.
Because instead of immediately abolishing every existing manifestation of polygamy in Israelite society, Mosaic law contains regulations addressing situations in which multiple wives existed.
Why?
Because biblical law sometimes regulates life in a fallen society without presenting every regulated condition as God's creational ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive key when discussing another marital issue—divorce.
In Matthew 19, religious leaders question Him about divorce.
Jesus does something remarkable.
He does not begin with Moses.
He goes farther back.
Back to creation.
He quotes Genesis.
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 says:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
kai esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Notice that word:
δύο — dyo
Two.
And:
μίαν — mian
One.
Jesus continues:
ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶν δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Then He says:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
When challenged about Moses permitting divorce, Jesus explains that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of human hearts, but adds:
“from the beginning it was not so.”
Those words give us a crucial biblical principle.
Permission within human brokenness is not necessarily the same thing as God's original design.
Read that again.
Because it reaches far beyond ancient marriage customs.
There are things God confronts immediately.
There are things He restrains.
There are things He regulates amid fallen social realities.
There are consequences He allows human beings to experience.
And through the unfolding story of redemption, He continually draws His people toward His holiness.
Even Israel's kings were explicitly warned about multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Wəlō yarbeh-lō nāšîm, wəlō yāsūr ləḇāḇō.
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
That warning becomes almost terrifying when you reach Solomon.
Because Solomon eventually becomes a living demonstration of the warning.
The king famous for wisdom became foolish precisely where God had warned Israel's kings.
First Kings 11 describes Solomon's many foreign wives and tells us that they turned his heart toward other gods.
The tragedy was not merely romantic excess.
It became spiritual adultery.
The man who built the temple allowed idols into his heart.
Think about that.
You can build something for God while quietly allowing something else to take God's place inside you.
You can know Scripture and still negotiate with desire.
You can possess extraordinary wisdom and still rationalize the one compromise that eventually conquers you.
Solomon is not merely an ancient warning about marriage.
He is a mirror.
Because every generation has its own version of multiplying wives.
Something God warned us about...
something culture normalizes...
something our flesh desires...
something we tell ourselves we can control.
Until one day...
it controls us.
And maybe this article stopped being about Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon several paragraphs ago.
Maybe now it is about you.
Maybe there is something in your life you have been defending simply because God has not struck you down for it.
Something you tolerate because judgment has not arrived.
Something you keep calling “grace” when grace has actually been calling you to repentance.
Be careful.
God's patience is not proof of God's approval.
That sentence can save someone's soul from years of unnecessary pain.
The patriarchs demonstrate something profoundly important about Scripture:
God's redemptive plan does not depend upon morally flawless human beings.
If it did...
Genesis would have ended very quickly.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Judah fell into sexual scandal.
Moses failed.
David committed devastating sins.
Solomon compromised.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
Yet God's promise kept moving.
Not because sin did not matter.
But because grace was greater than the sinners through whom God chose to work.
And all those fractured stories eventually move toward One who was not fractured.
Jesus Christ.
The faithful Son.
The spotless Lamb.
The true Bridegroom.
This is where the biblical picture of marriage becomes even more beautiful.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 that the union of husband and wife points beyond itself toward Christ and His Church.
Marriage was never merely about human companionship.
It carries a Gospel-shaped mystery.
Christ loves His Bride.
Christ gives Himself for His Bride.
Christ sanctifies His Bride.
Christ does not exploit His Bride.
He dies for her.
The ultimate answer to humanity's broken relationships is therefore not merely better relationship rules.
It is Christ.
Because our deepest problem has never simply been polygamy, divorce, lust, jealousy, adultery, or dysfunctional families.
Those are branches.
The root goes deeper.
The human heart departed from God.
And Jesus came to bring sinners home.
That is why Christianity is not the story of good people proving themselves worthy of God.
It is the story of sinners discovering they never were.
And then discovering something even more astonishing:
Jesus knew...
and came anyway.
Maybe your scandal looks nothing like Abraham's.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe your marriage is struggling.
Maybe pornography has been eating your soul in secret.
Maybe you crossed a boundary you promised yourself you never would.
Maybe resentment has turned your bedroom cold.
Maybe jealousy is poisoning you.
Maybe your family history is complicated.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe your children know a version of you that your church never sees.
Maybe you have been reading about dysfunctional biblical families because your own family feels painfully familiar.
Hear this clearly.
The Bible does not hide broken families because God does not need perfect backgrounds to create redeemed futures.
But grace is not permission to remain where sin left you.
Jesus does not merely forgive.
He transforms.
He calls adulterers to purity.
Liars to truth.
The proud to humility.
The sexually broken to holiness.
The bitter to forgiveness.
The hidden sinner into the light.
The dead...
to life.
This is the Gospel.
Not “God doesn't care how you live.”
And not “Fix yourself so God will love you.”
The Gospel says:
You could not rescue yourself.
So Christ came for you.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died the death sinners deserved.
He rose victorious.
And now forgiveness is offered not because your scandal was small...
but because His sacrifice was enough.
Repent.
Come home.
Stop hiding.
Stop using biblical characters' failures to justify what Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Abraham's failures cannot save you.
David's failures cannot excuse you.
Solomon's compromises cannot defend you.
Only Jesus can redeem you.
And perhaps that is why God allowed Scripture to show us these men exactly as they were.
Because if the Bible contained nothing but flawless heroes, people like us might eventually conclude there was no place in God's story for people like us.
But Scripture leaves the scars visible.
Then grace walks straight through them.
Be honest.

And if God has already brought you through relational wreckage, betrayal, sexual sin, family dysfunction, or a season you thought would destroy you, share what Christ has done. Someone reading your testimony may desperately need proof that failure does not have to write the final chapter.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Not merely to help an algorithm.
Somebody is wondering whether the Bible contradicts itself.
Somebody thinks their family is too broken for God.
Somebody has mistaken God's patience for permission.
Somebody needs Jesus.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from faith, gratitude, love, and a sincere desire to help Gospel ministry continue.
Pray.
Because somewhere tonight, another Abraham is discovering the cost of taking matters into his own hands.
Another Leah is wondering why she never feels chosen.
Another Hagar feels abandoned in the wilderness.
Another David is hiding a scandal.
Another Solomon thinks he can manage his compromise.
And another broken sinner is wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
The answer is standing at a cross with wounded hands.
Yes.
But He loves you too much to leave you unchanged.
The Bible never needed perfect patriarchs to prove that God was faithful. It needed a perfect Savior—and His name is Jesus.
